prompt_free_text:
This paper studies an interesting and timely problem: how to adapt concept bottleneck models built on top of foundation-model features when the deployment distribution shifts and only unlabeled target data are available. The paper’s central claim is that concept-based pipelines are not automatically robust under shift, even when the underlying foundation model is relatively strong, and that one can recover both accuracy and concept alignment through a three-stage adaptation procedure. Overall, I found the problem well motivated, the empirical phenomenon plausible and important, and the proposed method reasonably intuitive. At the same time, I have substantial reservations about the technical grounding, the clarity of some claims, and the strength of the empirical evidence relative to the paper’s broad conclusions.

The main strengths are clear. First, the paper addresses a genuinely underexplored intersection: concept bottleneck models, foundation models, and test-time/source-free adaptation. That combination is novel enough to be of interest to the community. Second, the paper identifies a useful practical point that is easy to overlook: even if a CBM is competitive in-domain, its bottleneck can become the weak link under shift, and interpretability does not imply robustness. This is a valuable message. Third, the proposed decomposition into concept-score alignment, classifier adaptation, and residual concept expansion is conceptually sensible. It maps naturally onto three failure modes: unstable concept projections, changed concept-label relations, and incomplete concept sets. Fourth, the experiments span several datasets and multiple CBM construction methods, which is better than evaluating only one bottleneck instantiation.

That said, I think the paper currently overstates both its formal contribution and the empirical support for some of its claims. My biggest concern is that the theoretical framing in Section 2 is not yet sufficiently rigorous or well aligned with the actual method. The definitions of “low-level shift” and “concept-level shift” are effectively defined relative to a chosen concept mapping h and classifier g, rather than as intrinsic properties of the data-generating process. In particular, low-level shift is defined by equality of concept-score distributions across domains, which is exactly what often fails in practice and is later called a failure mode. So the taxonomy risks becoming tautological: a shift is “low-level” if the concept representation is invariant, and if it is not invariant then the model exhibits a failure mode. Similarly, concept-level shift is defined by changed concept distributions but unchanged prediction distributions under a given g, which again depends on the model rather than the environment. This makes the formalism less explanatory than it first appears. The “complete concept set” definition is also quite weak and somewhat circular: existence of some g that equalizes prediction distributions across source and target does not by itself capture semantic completeness or sufficiency for label prediction. I would encourage the authors to either substantially sharpen this section or present it more modestly as an informal taxonomy rather than a formal characterization.

A related issue is that the method does not really follow from the formal development in a principled way. For example, CSA assumes access to class-conditional Gaussian statistics of source-domain concept scores, but this assumption is introduced operationally rather than justified by the earlier framework. The paper says source data are unavailable but source statistics are assumed available; this is reasonable in practice, but it weakens the “source-free” framing and should be discussed more explicitly. In many realistic deployments, storing per-class covariance matrices for concept scores may be acceptable, but it is still a form of source-side retained information. The paper should clarify exactly what artifacts from source training are allowed: concept bank, classifier weights, linear probe, zero-shot prompts, class-conditional means/covariances, and perhaps source hyperparameter tuning. This matters for fair comparison to prior source-free adaptation methods.

The pseudo-labeling strategy is another major point of concern. The method relies on pseudo-labels from an ensemble of zero-shot and linear-probe predictors on the frozen FM, selecting the more confident prediction. This is a strong external signal, and in some sense much of the adaptation power may come from the fact that the pseudo-labeler is already a strong non-interpretable classifier. If so, CONDA may be less “recovering” robustness from the CBM and more “distilling” a stronger FM-based predictor into the bottleneck at test time. That is not necessarily a flaw, but it changes the interpretation of the contribution. The paper should quantify pseudo-label quality and disentangle how much of the gain comes from the pseudo-labeler versus the adaptation objectives themselves. A particularly important baseline is to train/adapt a plain linear classifier on the same pseudo-labels and compare whether the concept bottleneck structure adds anything beyond constrained distillation. More broadly, because the pseudo-labeler uses both zero-shot and linear-probe predictions, the method may inherit their biases and may not be applicable when such predictors are weak or unavailable. The paper acknowledges this partially, but the dependence is stronger than the presentation suggests.

Empirically, the results are mixed in a way that deserves a more careful narrative. The paper emphasizes improvements “up to 28%” and alignment with non-interpretable classification, but Table 1 shows several cases where CONDA does not match the best non-interpretable baseline and several cases where it degrades strong CBMs. For example, on CIFAR100 with the Yeh et al. CBM, adaptation reduces both AVG and WG. On Camelyon17 with the Yeh et al. CBM, adaptation also hurts. On Waterbirds, CONDA improves CBMs substantially but still does not clearly surpass the non-interpretable LP baseline. On Metashift, the gains are impressive, but again the zero-shot baseline is already very strong. These nuances should be front and center. The current framing sometimes implies broad effectiveness, whereas the evidence supports a more conditional conclusion: CONDA often helps weaker or shift-misaligned CBMs, especially under concept-level shifts, but can hurt already strong CBMs and does not consistently close the gap to the best feature-based predictor.

This leads to a broader methodological concern: the paper compares adapted CBMs to unadapted zero-shot and linear-probe baselines, but not to adapted non-interpretable baselines under the same test-time adaptation setting. Since the paper’s practical claim is that CBMs can be adapted to recover performance under shift, the relevant question is not only whether adapted CBMs approach static LP/ZS, but whether they are competitive with standard TTA methods applied directly to the FM-based classifier. Without such baselines, it is hard to assess the price of interpretability. For example, how does CONDA compare to Tent, MEMO, CAFA, or simple pseudo-label fine-tuning applied to the LP head or to a shallow adapter on FM features? If a standard TTA baseline on the LP head outperforms CONDA by a large margin, then the contribution is mainly interpretability-preserving adaptation rather than robustness parity. That would still be valuable, but the paper should demonstrate it explicitly.

I also think the ablation evidence, at least from the main paper, is not yet sufficient. The component analysis suggests CSA helps more for low-level shifts and LPA/RCB more for concept-level shifts, which is plausible and interesting. However, the paper also notes that using only a subset of components can outperform the full method. This raises the question of whether the three-stage pipeline is over-engineered or whether a shift-type-aware gating mechanism is needed. Since the method is intended for deployment “in the wild,” one cannot assume prior knowledge of shift type. The paper should therefore either provide a criterion for deciding which components to activate, or show that the full method is robust enough across settings despite occasional underperformance. Right now, the evidence suggests that the full pipeline is not uniformly best.

There are also several technical details that need clarification or correction. The Mahalanobis distance expression in Section 3.1 appears to have a parenthesis typo. More importantly, covariance estimation in concept space may be unstable when the number of concepts is not small relative to per-class sample size; I assume some regularization or diagonal loading is used, but this is not discussed in the main text. Since the method depends critically on inverse covariances, numerical stability matters. The Gaussian assumption itself is fairly strong and may be especially questionable for concept scores derived from cosine-like projections of FM embeddings. It would strengthen the paper to include either empirical evidence that the assumption is adequate or an ablation comparing full covariance, diagonal covariance, and simpler moment matching objectives.

The residual concept bottleneck is appealing, but its interpretability story is not fully convincing yet. Adding randomly initialized residual concepts optimized with cross-entropy plus similarity/coherency regularization may improve accuracy, but whether these learned directions correspond to stable, human-meaningful concepts is less clear. The paper provides anecdotal examples on Waterbirds, which are encouraging, but stronger evidence is needed. For instance, how often do residual concepts receive coherent textual annotations across runs? Are they stable under random seeds? Do humans judge them as meaningful? Do they improve intervention utility, not just post hoc plausibility? Without such evidence, the residual branch may be better viewed as an accuracy-recovery mechanism with some interpretability regularization, rather than a guaranteed concept discovery module.

I also have concerns about the evaluation of interpretability. The paper claims that CONDA produces “concept-based interpretations better aligned with the test data,” but the evidence presented in the main text is qualitative and limited to one dataset. Since interpretability is a central motivation, I would expect at least one quantitative proxy: concept sparsity, concept coherency, concept completeness, intervention effectiveness, or human evaluation of concept relevance before and after adaptation. Even a simple measure such as overlap between top concepts and known spurious/background attributes versus object-centric attributes would help substantiate the claim.

Another issue is fairness of the CBM comparisons. The three CBM construction methods differ substantially in capacity and source-domain performance. In Table 1, the Yeh et al. method is often much stronger than the others even before adaptation, which makes adaptation gains harder to interpret. It would help to normalize for source-domain accuracy or concept-bank size, or at least report the number of concepts and residual concepts used for each method and dataset in the main paper. Otherwise, some gains may simply reflect that weaker CBMs have more room for improvement.

The paper’s use of AVG and WG is appropriate for shifted settings, especially Waterbirds and Metashift, but the definition of “group” seems to collapse to per-class accuracy in the text. For datasets like Waterbirds, worst-group accuracy usually refers to environment-defined groups, not classes. The paper says AVG is average per-class accuracy and WG is minimum per-class accuracy, which is unusual terminology for these benchmarks. This needs clarification because WG on Waterbirds and Metashift is typically a key robustness metric tied to spurious correlations. If the paper is instead reporting worst-class accuracy, that is a materially different metric and should not be conflated with standard worst-group accuracy.

I do want to emphasize that despite these criticisms, I think the paper has a promising core idea. The observation that CBMs need adaptation under shift is important, and the modular adaptation design is sensible. The strongest empirical story, in my view, is on concept-level shifts such as Waterbirds and Metashift, where adapting concept reliance and augmenting the concept bank are intuitively necessary and where the gains are substantial. If the paper narrowed its claims, strengthened baselines, and clarified the role of pseudo-labeling and source statistics, it could become a solid contribution.

For improvement, I would strongly recommend the following. First, add direct comparisons against standard TTA baselines applied to non-interpretable FM classifiers and, ideally, to the CBM logits without concept adaptation. Second, quantify pseudo-label accuracy and include a baseline that simply retrains the CBM head on pseudo-labels, as well as a baseline that distills the FM predictor into a linear or shallow model without concepts. Third, clarify the exact source-free assumptions and storage requirements. Fourth, provide more rigorous or at least more modest theoretical framing; the current formalism should not be oversold. Fifth, strengthen interpretability evaluation beyond anecdotes, especially for residual concepts. Sixth, clarify the WG metric and ensure consistency with benchmark conventions. Seventh, analyze failure cases where CONDA hurts performance, especially on already strong CBMs, and perhaps propose a confidence-based mechanism to skip harmful adaptation stages.

My overall assessment is that this is a novel and potentially impactful paper with a good problem formulation at the application level, but the current version falls short of the standard for a top-tier conference because the empirical validation is incomplete relative to the claims, the theoretical framing is not yet convincing, and several methodological choices need stronger justification. I would lean borderline to weak reject in its current form, while noting that a strengthened revision could become competitive.

If I were to summarize succinctly: the paper asks an important question and proposes a plausible solution, but it needs stronger baselines, clearer assumptions, and more careful claims about both theory and interpretability.

prompt_structured_json.summary: The paper studies test-time adaptation for concept bottleneck models (CBMs) built on top of foundation model features under distribution shift. It argues that CBMs, despite interpretability benefits, are not inherently robust after deployment. The proposed method, CONDA, adapts a deployed CBM using only unlabeled target data and no source data through three stages: concept-score alignment (CSA) that updates concept vectors using pseudo-labels and source-domain class-conditional concept statistics; linear probing adaptation (LPA) that updates the concept-to-label linear layer with pseudo-label cross-entropy and sparsity regularization; and a residual concept bottleneck (RCB) that adds new concept vectors to compensate for incomplete source concepts. Experiments on CIFAR10/100-C, Waterbirds, Metashift, and Camelyon17 with several CBM construction methods show substantial gains over unadapted CBMs in many settings, especially under concept-level shifts, and qualitative examples suggest adapted concepts better reflect target-domain correlations.
strengths: Addresses an interesting and underexplored problem: test-time adaptation for interpretable concept bottleneck pipelines built on foundation models.
The decomposition into three failure modes and corresponding adaptation modules is intuitive and provides a useful conceptual framework for thinking about CBMs under shift.
The method is source-free at adaptation time and uses only unlabeled target data, which is practically relevant.
Empirical evaluation spans multiple datasets, multiple shift types, multiple backbones, and multiple CBM construction methods, which strengthens the practical case for the approach.
Results show large improvements over unadapted CBMs in several challenging settings, especially Waterbirds and Metashift, where concept-level shifts are severe.
The paper includes some interpretability-oriented analysis, including discussion of how concept reliance changes after adaptation and how residual concepts may capture missing semantics.
weaknesses: The theoretical framing of shift types and completeness is largely definitional and does not yield formal guarantees, identifiable conditions, or testable consequences; several definitions are stronger than needed and somewhat disconnected from the algorithm.

The method relies heavily on pseudo-label quality from zero-shot/linear-probe FM predictors, so gains may largely inherit robustness from non-interpretable predictors rather than arise from principled concept adaptation.

The comparison set is incomplete for the claimed problem: there is little direct comparison against strong generic test-time adaptation baselines applied to the equivalent linear classifier or to CBM logits/features, making it hard to isolate the benefit of the concept-specific design.

Some empirical claims are overstated relative to the table: adaptation does not consistently match or exceed non-interpretable baselines, and in several cases adapted CBMs remain clearly below LP/ZS or even degrade relative to the best unadapted CBM.

Interpretability claims are suggestive but not rigorously evaluated; there is no quantitative human-grounded or faithfulness-based assessment showing that adapted/residual concepts are truly more meaningful rather than merely more predictive.

The method introduces several extra ingredients and hyperparameters (Gaussian statistics, pseudo-label ensemble, three-stage optimization, residual branch regularizers), raising concerns about sensitivity and reproducibility despite limited evidence in the main paper.

The source-free assumption is softened by requiring access to source-domain class-conditional Gaussian statistics of concept scores; depending on the setting, this may be nontrivial auxiliary information not available in standard source-free adaptation setups.
methodological_flaws: The formal definition of low-level shift in Eq. (2) assumes the concept-score distribution is exactly unchanged across domains. This is not a property of the shift alone but of the pair (feature extractor, concept mapping). Many nominally low-level corruptions will alter concept scores in practice. Thus the taxonomy conflates semantic shift type with model invariance and weakens the scientific logic of the failure-mode analysis.

Definition 1 of concept completeness is problematic: it defines completeness via existence of a classifier whose prediction distributions match across domains, rather than via sufficiency of concepts for labels. Equality of prediction distributions is weaker than preserving correct conditional label relationships and can hold for degenerate reasons. This makes the notion of 'incomplete concept set' mathematically misaligned with standard completeness/sufficiency notions.

The CSA objective is only loosely justified as approximating class-conditional distribution alignment. Minimizing log(D_intra/D_inter) based on Mahalanobis distances to source Gaussians does not correspond to minimizing any explicit divergence between source and target class-conditional distributions. The Gaussian assumption and ratio loss are heuristic, not derived from the stated alignment objective.

CSA depends on source-domain Gaussian statistics estimated in the original concept space, but concept vectors are then changed during adaptation. Once C changes, the original source statistics for C_s phi(x_s) are no longer the correct source statistics for C phi(x_s). Using fixed source means/covariances while optimizing C is mathematically inconsistent with the stated goal of matching target concept scores to source concept-score distributions under the adapted concept bank.

The Mahalanobis formulation may be numerically unstable or ill-posed when the number of concepts is large relative to per-class source samples, yet the paper does not discuss covariance regularization, shrinkage, or invertibility assumptions. This is an empirical validity concern, especially for datasets with many classes such as CIFAR100.

The pseudo-labeling protocol may leak substantial supervision from stronger non-interpretable models into the CBM adaptation. Since pseudo-labels are chosen from an ensemble of zero-shot and linear-probe predictors, improvements cannot be cleanly attributed to concept adaptation alone. A stronger analysis would compare against directly using those pseudo-label providers or adapting a non-concept linear head with the same pseudo-labels.

The online adaptation protocol evaluates on the same batch used for adaptation, which is standard in some TTA work but can inflate apparent gains and makes results sensitive to batch order and batch composition. The paper does not sufficiently analyze order sensitivity or compare episodic vs online adaptation in the main results.

The residual branch in Eq. (5) effectively turns the model into a larger linear classifier over FM features factorized as W_con C_con. This blurs the distinction between concept-based adaptation and simply increasing linear model capacity. Without stronger constraints or comparisons to an equally parameterized residual linear probe, the empirical gains from RCB do not establish that the added dimensions function as interpretable concepts rather than generic latent directions.

There are apparent inconsistencies in equation references and notation (e.g., LPA refers to predictions from Eq. (3) though the target CBM is defined later as Eq. (5); Appendix table also references Eq. (3) for target CBM). While minor, such issues reduce confidence in the mathematical presentation.

Empirically, some adapted results are worse than unadapted CBMs (e.g., CIFAR100 and Camelyon17 for the Yeh et al. CBM), and some adapted CBMs remain far below LP/ZS. The paper's broad claim of aligning CBM performance with non-interpretable classification is therefore not uniformly supported by the presented evidence.
